blocks.html: Concurrency starts with a basic fact: threads in the same process share memory.
blocks.text: Concurrency starts with a basic fact: threads in the same process share memory.

blocks.html: Concurrency exists whenever multiple threads can make progress independently and their execution can overlap.
blocks.text: Concurrency exists whenever multiple threads can make progress independently and their execution can overlap.

blocks.html: When multiple running threads use the same memory space, the OS switches between the threads really really fast and in an unpredictable manner, leading to indeterministic results.
blocks.text: When multiple running threads use the same memory space, the OS switches between the threads really really fast and in an unpredictable manner, leading to indeterministic results.

blocks.html: Even the debugging is really tough in such systems, because the switching manner is unpredictable, therefore the same set of actions may not lead to same results.
blocks.text: Even the debugging is really tough in such systems, because the switching manner is unpredictable, therefore the same set of actions may not lead to same results.

blocks.html: So, concurrency comes with its own problems.
blocks.text: So, concurrency comes with its own problems.

blocks.html: What looks like one instruction on the source code level, could be a multiple machine instructions.
blocks.text: What looks like one instruction on the source code level, could be a multiple machine instructions.

blocks.html: a = b + c; may look like one instruction on the source code level, but at machine level these are many instructions.
blocks.text: a = b + c; may look like one instruction on the source code level, but at machine level these are many instructions.

blocks.html: To deal with the concurrency problems, programming languages/libraries/frameworks etc, provide some tools. The most common ones are listed. One thing to clear is that, the tools listed below, are provided by the language/library/framework so we do not need to implement them, we need to only consume them.
blocks.text: To deal with the concurrency problems, programming languages/libraries/frameworks etc, provide some tools. The most common ones are listed. One thing to clear is that, the tools listed below, are provided by the language/library/framework so we do not need to implement them, we need to only consume them.

blocks.html: Atomics
blocks.text: Atomics

blocks.html: Atomics are the lowest-level tool for concurrency: operations that complete in a single, indivisible step.
blocks.text: Atomics are the lowest-level tool for concurrency: operations that complete in a single, indivisible step.

blocks.html: No thread can see a half-done state.
blocks.text: No thread can see a half-done state.

blocks.html:
If two threads do 
atomic_increment(x)
 at the same time, 
x
 goes up by 2, never 1. No race condition, no mutex needed. The CPU guarantees it (basically the language does but you can say CPU).
blocks.text: If two threads do atomic_increment(x) at the same time, x goes up by 2, never 1. No race condition, no mutex needed. The CPU guarantees it (basically the language does but you can say CPU).

blocks.html: Therefore, when using atomics, no need to put any other thing like counter, locks, flags, pointers, etc.
blocks.text: Therefore, when using atomics, no need to put any other thing like counter, locks, flags, pointers, etc.

blocks.html: You can search internet to know if a specific language provides it or not, and if yes, then how.
blocks.text: You can search internet to know if a specific language provides it or not, and if yes, then how.

blocks.html: Locks
blocks.text: Locks

blocks.html: Locks guarantee mutual exclusion: only one thread can run a block of code at a time. If atomics are a scalpel for single variables, locks are a sledgehammer for protecting whole chunks of logic and multiple variables together.
blocks.text: Locks guarantee mutual exclusion: only one thread can run a block of code at a time. If atomics are a scalpel for single variables, locks are a sledgehammer for protecting whole chunks of logic and multiple variables together.

blocks.html:
You use them when atomics aren’t enough. Example: transferring money needs 
accountA -= 100
 and 
accountB += 100
 to happen together.
blocks.text: You use them when atomics aren’t enough. Example: transferring money needs accountA -= 100 and accountB += 100 to happen together.

blocks.html: Deadlock, popular problem, is a problem that may arise if locks are not used intelligently.
blocks.text: Deadlock, popular problem, is a problem that may arise if locks are not used intelligently.

blocks.html: Exclusion does not mean that only one thread can do a operation at time. It can be more than one threads. The only thing exclusion here means is that a set (set of one or more) of threads doing an operation, does not let any other thread outside the set do anything.
blocks.text: Exclusion does not mean that only one thread can do a operation at time. It can be more than one threads. The only thing exclusion here means is that a set (set of one or more) of threads doing an operation, does not let any other thread outside the set do anything.

blocks.html: For example: 10 threads reading (reading means reading no writing) a data, prevent any thread to write.
blocks.text: For example: 10 threads reading (reading means reading no writing) a data, prevent any thread to write.

blocks.html: What does mutual mean, if thread A prevents B from interfering, then on B’s turn, B would prevent A, provided they are doing same operations.
blocks.text: What does mutual mean, if thread A prevents B from interfering, then on B’s turn, B would prevent A, provided they are doing same operations.

blocks.html: Mutexes
blocks.text: Mutexes

blocks.html: Mutexes are special types of locks. In which only one thread is allowed to do the operation at a time. Whether it be read or write.
blocks.text: Mutexes are special types of locks. In which only one thread is allowed to do the operation at a time. Whether it be read or write.

blocks.html: 10 threads reading a data simultaneously, and preventing any thread to write data is not mutex.
blocks.text: 10 threads reading a data simultaneously, and preventing any thread to write data is not mutex.

blocks.html: The mutex doesn't care what you're doing. It only cares how many. And the number must be one and one only.
blocks.text: The mutex doesn't care what you're doing. It only cares how many. And the number must be one and one only.

blocks.html: When people say "lock" in casual conversation, 90% of the time they mean "mutex". Because mutex = the simplest, most common lock.
blocks.text: When people say "lock" in casual conversation, 90% of the time they mean "mutex". Because mutex = the simplest, most common lock.

blocks.html: That's because a mutex IS the canonical example of a lock.
blocks.text: That's because a mutex IS the canonical example of a lock.

blocks.html: Semaphores
blocks.text: Semaphores

blocks.html: Semaphore = a lock with a counter. Instead of "1 thread only", it says "N threads allowed at once". And, a few more nuances.
blocks.text: Semaphore = a lock with a counter. Instead of "1 thread only", it says "N threads allowed at once". And, a few more nuances.

blocks.html: N threads allowed at once, means N permits that can be given.
blocks.text: N threads allowed at once, means N permits that can be given.

blocks.html: A counter variable is used to store the free permits. Initially counter = N
blocks.text: A counter variable is used to store the free permits. Initially counter = N

blocks.html:
When a thread acquires a permit, better to say acquires the semaphore,
counter--
is done. When thread releases a permit
counter++
is done.
blocks.text: When a thread acquires a permit, better to say acquires the semaphore, counter-- is done. When thread releases a permit counter++ is done.

blocks.html: Here is a catch, if A acquires a permit, it does not mean A releases the permit. How??
blocks.text: Here is a catch, if A acquires a permit, it does not mean A releases the permit. How??

blocks.html: P and V names were given to the operations by Dijkstra. Dijkstra invented semaphores in 1965. And Mutexes came later, because of issues in semaphores.

blocks.html: The names confused me.

blocks.html: How can wait and acquire mean the same thing?
blocks.text: How can wait and acquire mean the same thing?

blocks.html:
When we do
semaphore.acquire()
, the thread may not immediately acquire the semaphore, it may wait, and if it has to wait, it will sleep.
blocks.text: When we do semaphore.acquire(), the thread may not immediately acquire the semaphore, it may wait, and if it has to wait, it will sleep.

blocks.html:
semaphore.acquire()
means wait until you get a chance to acquire, and acquire the moment you get the chance. At source code level we do not write wait and acquire separately. And that is why wait/acquire mean the same thing at the source code level.
blocks.text: semaphore.acquire() means wait until you get a chance to acquire, and acquire the moment you get the chance. At source code level we do not write wait and acquire separately. And that is why wait/acquire mean the same thing at the source code level.

blocks.html:
Similarly,
signal()
 / 
release()
 means I'm done with my permit. Increment the count, and wake someone up if they're waiting.
blocks.text: Similarly, signal() / release() means I'm done with my permit. Increment the count, and wake someone up if they're waiting.

blocks.html: One more catch.
blocks.text: One more catch.

blocks.html: With semaphores there is no ownership. With mutexes there is. That’s the biggest behavioral difference.
blocks.text: With semaphores there is no ownership. With mutexes there is. That’s the biggest behavioral difference.

blocks.html: Mutex: ownership is enforced
blocks.text: Mutex: ownership is enforced

blocks.html:
The OS/library remembers which thread called 
lock()
. Only that same thread is allowed to call 
unlock()
.
blocks.text: The OS/library remembers which thread called lock(). Only that same thread is allowed to call unlock().

blocks.html: If Thread A dies while holding the mutex, you get a deadlock or "abandoned mutex" error. The system knows who the owner was.
blocks.text: If Thread A dies while holding the mutex, you get a deadlock or "abandoned mutex" error. The system knows who the owner was.

blocks.html: Semaphore: no ownership, just a counter
blocks.text: Semaphore: no ownership, just a counter

blocks.html:
The semaphore is just an integer. It doesn't track who did 
acquire()
. Anyone can 
release()
. This is an issue in semaphores, but if used carefully acts as a feature.
blocks.text: The semaphore is just an integer. It doesn't track who did acquire(). Anyone can release(). This is an issue in semaphores, but if used carefully acts as a feature.
